content.thinking:
I'm drafting the postmortem, noting the monthly-spend-feature flag flip at 23:47 caused p99 latency to spike from 199ms to as high as 1300-1700ms while error rates stayed nearly flat, and the incident resolved in about six minutes once the flag was reverted. Now I'm outlining the assumptions behind that analysis.

I should avoid restating the given cost or impact figures as if I computed them myself, and shouldn't offer my own numbers either. I can safely describe the timeline factually — onset around 23:47, recovery around 23:53, roughly six minutes — while framing error rate and latency qualitatively rather than as precise stats I derived. For the executive summary, I'll keep it generic, referring to "the shop's account pages" and "a newly enabled feature" rather than specific component names.

assumptions: Causation is inferred from timing plus the successful revert, not from profiling or tracing: nobody established what inside the new code path is slow.
The latency figures (199ms baseline, 390ms at 23:47, 1300-1700ms at full rollout) come from the investigator's reading of the per-minute metrics; they were not independently verified.

The competing hypothesis - that the flag merely exposed a slow upstream dependency rather than being slow itself - was never tested. It was rated low-confidence only because the logs name no upstream service and show no timeouts or 5xx errors; absence of such log lines is weak evidence.

The steady trickle of ClientDisconnected errors on account pages is present throughout the 30 minutes before onset and is treated as pre-existing background noise unrelated to this incident, though it was not investigated.
Recovery is taken from the metrics returning to baseline at 23:53 and the mitigation agent's check at 23:54; no independent confirmation (e.g. user-facing checks) was performed.

A revert of this same flag was recorded as unsuccessful on a prior incident (55f4ab31-5373-4ab7-92f3-ceec23c70671), and that history was used to deprioritise it here before it was acted on anyway. Why it worked this time and not then is unexplained.
No permanent fix was produced: the code-fix agent ran out of tokens before proposing one, so the only thing standing between the service and a recurrence is the flag being left off.
input.executive_summary: Late on 22 September, a new account-spend feature was switched on for shoppers. From the moment it began serving traffic (23:47 UTC), account pages became much slower to load — response times went from roughly a fifth of a second to several seconds at the slow end — and the degradation grew as the feature reached all users. Monitoring alerted at 23:52, the automated responder identified the newly enabled feature as the cause and switched it back off, and the service was back to normal speed by 23:53. The whole disruption lasted about six minutes. Requests largely still succeeded — the failure rate over the window barely moved from its normal level, as separately measured — so the impact on shoppers was slowness on account pages rather than outright errors, and no orders or data were lost. The feature remains switched off; it needs to be made faster before it is enabled again.
input.root_cause: The `monthly-spend-feature` feature flag was rolled out from off to on; the first minute in which any request evaluated the flag as "on" (23:47) is the same minute p99 latency left baseline (~199ms → ~390ms, then multi-second as the rollout reached 100%). No code or config deploy touched io-shop in the preceding 24 hours, and turning the flag back off returned latency to baseline, so the slow path newly exposed by the flag is the cause.
